paragraphs.text: From thy lofty top and towering state, as the head city of the world. {a}
paragraphs.anchor: Come down.

paragraphs.text: {b} As a mourner. {Job 2:8; Job 42:6} So Judea, being subdued by Vespasian, was pictured upon money coined by him as a handmaid sitting on the ground. Sic ruet alto a culmine Roma!
paragraphs.anchor: Sit in the dust.

paragraphs.text: Thou that hast never yet been subdued. So Venice hath for her motto, ‘Intacta maneo’; so Cologne-upon-Rhine is called ‘the virgin city.’
paragraphs.anchor: O virgin daughter of Babylon.

paragraphs.text: So as queens use to be - Cleopatra, for instance.
paragraphs.anchor: Thou shalt no more be called tender and delicate.

paragraphs.text: {a} Sic transit gloria mundi., So fleeting is the glory of the world.
{b} Cyrillus wrote εν τω οκοτει.

As the most abject slaves used to do, qui in pistrinum trudebantur. Neither is this an end of thy sorrows; for out of the mill house thou must be carried captive into a far country, and therefore, in order thereunto,
paragraphs.anchor: Take the millstone.

paragraphs.text: Cast away thy diadem.
paragraphs.anchor: Uncover thy locks.

paragraphs.text: Denuda turpitudinem, the Vulgate rendereth it; that thou mayest pass through the waters naked and squalid into captivity.
paragraphs.anchor: Make bare thy leg.

paragraphs.text: Thou shalt be stripped, and worse dealt with - the ordinary lot of women prisoners. At the sack of Magdeburg by Monsieur Tilly, ladies, gentlewomen, and others, like beasts and dogs, being naked and coupled together, were led into the woods, and there ravished. Such as resisted, the soldiers stripped naked, whipped them, cropped their ears, and so sent them home again.
paragraphs.anchor: Thy nakedness shall be uncovered.

paragraphs.text: But as a lion rather; thou shalt have vengeance without mixture of mercy. See 2Sa 7:24 Isa 13:6; Isa 27:7-8 Hos 5:14. Men use sometimes to deal favourably with women, but they shall not do so with thee. {a}
paragraphs.anchor: I will not meet thee as a man.

paragraphs.text: {a} Absque omni humanitatis contemperatione. - Scult. Tractabo te pro divina potentia mea. - Piscat.
This comes in by way of parenthesis, for the comfort of God’s poor people.
paragraphs.anchor: As for our Redeemer, &c.

paragraphs.text: Here he threateneth Babylon with loss of her former fame; she shall be buried in obscurity and oblivion, as out of sight and out of mind, no longer called the ‘lady of kingdoms,’ but a wretched drudge, ut de Hecuba tradunt tragici.
paragraphs.anchor: Sit thou silent.

paragraphs.text: Heb., Thou shalt not add to be called. Oecolampadius senseth it thus, Thou wast wont to be called the lady of kingdoms, now they shall call thee, Non adiecies, as desperate and irrecoverable. And why?
paragraphs.anchor: For thou shalt no more be called.

paragraphs.text: See on Zec 1:15.
paragraphs.anchor: I was wroth.

paragraphs.text: God is his people’s inheritance, and they are his; but now, for their sins, he had dealt with them as with a profane and unclean thing.
paragraphs.anchor: I have polluted mine inheritance.

paragraphs.text: Heb., Thou didst set them no bowels. Cruelty cries for vengeance. See Jer 50:17; Jer 51:24.
paragraphs.anchor: Thou didst show them no mercy.

paragraphs.text: Who should have been borne with for their age and weakness.
paragraphs.anchor: Upon the ancient.

paragraphs.text: Presumption precedeth destruction. {Psa 10:6 Rev 18:7}
paragraphs.anchor: I shall be a lady for ever.

paragraphs.text: The daughter of pride is security, and pleasure is her niece. {Isa 47:8}
paragraphs.anchor: So that thou didst not lay these things to thy heart.

paragraphs.text: Heb., Her latter end. Memorare novissima tua, et in aeternum non peccabis. See Lam 1:4.
paragraphs.anchor: Nor didst remember the latter end of it.

paragraphs.text: Delisatula; It is not good to take pleasure in pleasure; no, not to go as far here as we may. Verecunda sunt omnia initia peecati, Sin seemeth modest at first, &c.
paragraphs.anchor: Thou that art given to pleasure.

paragraphs.text: sc., The lady of the world. Heathen Rome was called by the heathens, Terrarum dea gentiumque. Rome Papal saith as much. {Rev 17:4}
paragraphs.anchor: Thou sayest in thine heart, I am

paragraphs.text: i.e., None worth speaking of. The Jesuits brag in like sort of their transcendent learning, and profess skill beyond the periphery of possible knowledge.
paragraphs.anchor: And none else besides me

paragraphs.text: i.e., Be bereft of my monarchy, which is, as it were, my husband.
paragraphs.anchor: I shall not sit as a widow

paragraphs.text: I shall not cease to subdue countries and kingdoms, which are added unto me as so many children.
paragraphs.anchor: Neither shall I know the loss of children.

paragraphs.text: Accidit in puncto, &c. Babylon was suddenly taken in one night, as the prophet had foretold, {Isa 21:9} and as the history testifieth {Dan 5:30} Periit inter pocula.
paragraphs.anchor: But these two things shall come upon thee in a moment.

paragraphs.text: Thy taking upon thee to divine of each man’s life and fortune by the stars and horoscope, for which profession the Chaldeans were famous. But what a madness was it in Cardanus, who by the like skill went about to demonstrate that it was fatal to our Saviour Christ to die the death of the cross. {a}
paragraphs.anchor: For the multitude of thy sorceries.

paragraphs.text: {a} Alsted. Encycl., lib. xxx. cap. 10.
God calleth that "wickedness" which they counted wisdom.
paragraphs.anchor: Thou hast trusted in thy wickedness.

paragraphs.text: Ne Deus quidem novit rationes mess. Graceless men, having hid God from themselves, think also to hide themselves from God.
paragraphs.anchor: None seeth me.

paragraphs.text: Thy magical arts and practices. Quantus artifex pereo? quadrabit in te peritum et periturum.
paragraphs.anchor: Thy wisdom and thy knowledge.

paragraphs.text: An evil, "an only evil," {as Eze 7:5} both unexpected and inexpiable; such as thou canst neither avoid nor abide.
paragraphs.anchor: Therefore shall evil come upon thee.

paragraphs.text: {a} Try thine utmost skill, and let us see what thou canst do for thyself. This is spoken in way of derision.
paragraphs.anchor: Stand now with thine enchantments.

paragraphs.text: But found them to be no better than toilsome toys, quae nec ignoranti nocent, nec scientem iuvant, Against judiciary astrology, see Aug. De Civ. Dei, lib. v. cap. 1-5.
paragraphs.anchor: Wherein thou hast laboured from thy youth.

paragraphs.text: {a} Hinc divinatores per antonomasiam Chaldaei appellati.

As all such are sure to be, with a woe to boot, as "take counsel, but not of God; and that cover with a covering, but not by his Spirit, that they may add sin to sin" {Isa 30:1} Thus do those vain astrologers, that pretend to read men’s fates and fortunes in the heavens, velut in Minervae peplo, and thence to foretell good and evil. But experience frequently confuteth them, as it did Abraham the Jew, who foretold by the stars the coming of their Messiah, A.D. 1464; and Albumazar, a Mohammedan wizard, who predicted an end of the Christian religion, A.D. 1460 at utmost. A great flood was foretold by these diviners to occur in the year 1524, cum planetae comitia in piscibus celebrarent. This caused the prior of St Bartholomew’s, in London, wise manlike, to go and build him a house at Harrow-on-the-hill, for his better security. {a}
paragraphs.anchor: Thou art wearied in the multitude of thy counsels.

paragraphs.text: Save thee if they can: but Belshazzar found they could not, though he called for them all, {Dan 5:7-8} and they likely had promised him an everlasting monarchy - as some did the Romans imperium sine fine, but falsely; for now the Roman empire is at a very low ebb, and who shall be emperor is much questioned. {b}
paragraphs.anchor: Stand up, and save thee.

paragraphs.text: {a} Hollinsh. in 1524.
{b} This was written, Sept. 19, 1637.
As dried stubble. {Nah 1:10} {See Trapp on "Nah 1:10"}
paragraphs.anchor: Behold, they shall be as stubble.

paragraphs.text: Much less others.
paragraphs.anchor: They shall not deliver themselves.

paragraphs.text: Like a fire of flax, which is soon extinct, and leaves no embers or cinders behind it. In a spiritual sense, it may be said of most of our hearts and houses as here, There is not a coal to warm at. Deest ignis, as Father Latimer was wont to say; the fire of zeal is wanting, that flame of God. {Son 8:6}
paragraphs.anchor: There shall not be a coal to warm at.

paragraphs.text: But all in vain; viz., with thy wizards and diviners, those deceivers of the people, concerning whom Cato once said, Potest Augur Augurem videre et non ridere? {a} Can those fellows look one on another and not laugh, when they consider how they deceive people, and cheat them of their moneys? Hence they are called merchants also in the next words, as some think, qui non tam coeli rationem quam coelati argenti ducunt. {b} Such money merchants hath mystical Babylon also not a few. {Rev 18:11} Non desunt Antichristo sui Augures et malifici, saith Oecolampadius; Antichrist hath those abroad that trade with him and for him; these shall be "cast alive with him into the burning lake," {Rev 19:20} and though they wander, yet not so wide as to miss hell.
paragraphs.anchor: Thus shall they be unto thee with whom thou hast laboured.

paragraphs.text: {a} Cic. De Divinat., lib. ii.
{b} Cic. orat. iv. in Ver.
